items.title: 68252_Jay Cee
items.q: He mentioned Langston Hughes and he and Langston writing something together.

ctx.x: J. C. mentioned to me that between 1915 and 1918 he was running an elevator in New York City in the building where Bert Williams either lived or worked. He later mentioned that in the '20s Bert Williams lived at 134th and 7th Avenue. When I asked him what Harlem was like then, he said, 'It was the real Harlem back in the days of Billie Holiday and the Cha-Cha Club on 7th Avenue. It was a wide open village where people used to roam in perfect safety, people of all nationalities.'

He also indicated that Lenox Avenue was the last street to get rid of the trolley. He mentioned Langston Hughes and he and Langston writing something together. J. C. was disappointed about something in Langston and dropped the relationship. He did tell me that Langston initiated it. He still has the papers, the poem and the music in Wortsborough.

During this conversation he made one of his typical J. C. remarks, quote, "Don't let the same bee sting you twice." I found a real absence of ego in J. C. Johnson, and I think it's important to record this. The only time he ever, quote, "blew his own horn," so to speak, was when he mentioned the story of himself and Langston Hughes. And he said, quote, "I was running kind of hot myself when Langston autographed a book and sent it to me. Then he sent me his second book and asked to get together on something." End…
